chapter: The band's later history and Cootie Williams
title: Union, local bands, and Charlie and Frank Jackson
summary: Pope organized the musicians' union in Mobile; he has not played in 25 years; he recalls Charlie the pressing-shop trumpeter and Frank Jackson.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Are they professional musicians or do they have another job now? They don't play music.
Yes. Are they members of the union or are they...
Yes, they're all members of the union. They're all members of the union. I organized the American Federation of Musicians. In fact, I had it organized right here in Mobile.
Yes. I suppose some of them play in dance bands now, do they? Yes. Local dance bands?

Yes, I think so. Quite a few of them. But back in my days, we always had four or five orchestras in Mobile. Now, I think they have one. Yes. That's normal. I haven't heard of them myself. In fact, I've given up music now. It's been 25 years now.
I haven't played at all. In fact, you don't own an instrument. Yes.

A friend of ours in New Orleans, Bill Matthews, a trombone player, has his own band. And he told us a few names to look up. One man, he didn't remember his last name. He said, Charlie, a trumpet player, had a pressing shop on Davis Avenue down near town. What kind of shop? He's not pressing, press closed. That's Charlie. That's Charlie. That's Charlie. Yes, he's dead. And I couldn't look at him. Yes, he made it. And another man he mentioned to see was Frank Jackson, a band.

Frank Jackson, he played with me. He played with you? He played with me. Is he still living? In my orchestra. Yes, but he's living in South Carolina somewhere. Oh, he's not here then. Yeah, Mobile. Yes. Very good. And I don't know of anyone else now that's around that could give me any information.
